title: Data-driven learning in dynamic pricing using adaptive optimization
contribution: Models demand learning in finite-inventory pricing as adaptive robust optimization with a data-driven, policy-dependent uncertainty set. A hierarchical inner approximation is solved as a mixed-binary conic program, and it beats myopic and certainty-equivalent pricing on synthetic instances.
problem_entry: RO+DA (AP: revenue management). The demand curve is unknown and only a sales history exists. Most studies assume the curve is known (p. 3); Bayesian models are intractable and tied to conjugate priors (p. 5); robust pricing leaves no room for learning (p. 6). Two questions: (a) model demand uncertainty from data; (b) price to balance exploration and exploitation (p. 4).
key_idea: Learning as a property of the uncertainty set. The prior set holds every (alpha, beta) not falsified by the data under a norm-bounded residual (eq. (4), p. 13; set-membership estimation, Remark 4, p. 16). Future price-demand paths form a policy-dependent set U(pi) (eq. (5), p. 15). Prices are functions of the observed history, and worst-case profit is maximized over policies (DP, p. 18).
assumptions: Linear demand with ||eps||_p <= eta, p in {1, 2, inf}, and no distribution (p. 10). (A1) the model is valid, with p and eta known; (A2) the data set is bounded with a nonempty interior (p. 10). Linearity is defended over a moderate price range, and eta is admitted to be hard to set (pp. 10-11). Holding and backlog costs (p. 9); discrete prices (p. 24). Two synthetic instances with four historical points each (pp. 35-36).
proof_devices: Minimax theorem: with h = b = 0 and beta <= 0 a static robust policy is optimal (Proposition 1, p. 20; EC.1, p. 46). Otherwise, a two-period counterexample (Proposition 2, p. 20; EC.2, p. 46).

Approximation hierarchy: stage aggregation with a reduced information vector (pp. 21-22); K candidate strategies (pp. 23-24); piecewise-constant binary rules on a preselected box partition (pp. 25-26).
RO duality plus big-M linearization give a mixed-binary conic program. It is conservative for p in [1, inf] and exact for p in {1, inf} (Proposition 3, pp. 28-29; EC.3, pp. 49-50).
Size is polynomial for fixed |S| and exponential in M otherwise. Remedies: binary-encoded breakpoints and lifted partitions (pp. 29-30).
experiments: CPLEX 12.6, Core i7-920, 24 GB (p. 35). Learning gain over the static robust policy: above 73% in under 3 s, all frontier problems under 10 s, about -10% at |S| = 1 and M <= 2 (pp. 37-39). Out of sample: +31.5% worst case and +9.2% mean, but up to $223 lost on some draws (p. 39). Folding horizon against certainty-equivalent and myopic pricing: worst-case loss -76.6% and -92.8%, mean +1.28% and +4.52%, tail equal to the perfect-information policy (pp. 40-42). Synthetic data only.
positioning: Sets aside Bayesian learning, learning by classical estimation, and robust pricing without learning (pp. 4-6). Calls itself a data-driven, distribution-free paradigm (p. 6).
writing: Numbered contributions (pp. 7-8). Four 'to the best of our knowledge' priority claims (pp. 8, 15, 16, 29). No conclusion section beyond the conclusions from the experiments (p. 42).
limits_future: The approximation is conservative, and its size is exponential in M when |S| is free (p. 29). Eta and the norm must be known (p. 10). Synthetic data only, and no gap to DP itself (pp. 36-42). Future work: finite adaptability with decision-dependent sets (Remark 9, p. 25). Heuristic 4 evidence: the negative gain and the $223 loss are printed (pp. 37, 39).

method_links.note: Learning-and-earning, owned by the Bayesian and dual-control traditions, is rewritten as adaptive RO and brought into the mixed-binary conic class. It gets there only through a conservative approximation hierarchy. Exactness (p in {1, inf}) and the size explosion are printed.

The value of learning is priced as a learning gain over the static robust policy. It is drawn as an efficient frontier against solver time over the design knobs M and |S|, and the bad case (about -10%) is printed. The conservatism knob eta is left to the seller.
Coarser partitions warm-start finer ones, and times are reported cumulatively. Solver, version and machine are stated. There is no incumbent heuristic as warm start and no gap.
Decisions are scored by profit distributions (mean, VaR, CVaR) against the two rules commonly used in practice and a perfect-information bound. The instances are synthetic, with no owner.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: learning as a decision-dependent uncertainty set
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Exploration is modelled by letting prices shape a set-membership uncertainty set of future price-demand paths; exploitation by decision rules on the observed history. The authors claim it is the first model of this type.
Learning gain against solver time over the design knobs M and |S|: an efficient frontier, convergence at M = 4, and a negative bad case. S117 makes the same move (Tables 2-3, 5-6).

transferable: Build the uncertainty set as all parameters not falsified by the data under a norm-bounded residual. Prior and posterior sets keep the same conic form and always contain the truth (pp. 7, 13-16).
Before building adaptivity, prove when a static robust policy is optimal (minimax theorem), and give a two-period counterexample otherwise (p. 20; EC.1-EC.2, p. 46).

Solve an intractable adaptive problem in steps: aggregate stages, summarize the history by a few statistics, choose among K candidate strategies, warm-start finer partitions from coarser ones, and plot the gain-time efficient frontier (pp. 21-29, 38).
Judge robust policies on the downside (worst case, VaR, CVaR) in a folding-horizon simulation. Compare against certainty-equivalent and myopic rules and a perfect-information bound (pp. 40-42).

quotes.text: This construction enables us to unify optimization and (dynamic) estimation.
while the adaptive policy may yield up to $223 less than the myopic policy, it yields higher profits with probability greater than 81.6%

title: The trimmed lasso: Sparsity and robustness
contribution: Studies the trimmed Lasso as an exact penalty for best subset selection with direct control of sparsity. Interprets it as the min-min robust counterpart of SLOPE. Shows that it strictly subsumes bounded separable penalties such as the clipped Lasso. Compares DC, ADMM and convex-envelope heuristics against MIO certificates.
problem_entry: ML+IO (RO lens). Separable nonconvex penalties bridge the Lasso and best subset selection but give no direct control of sparsity (pp. 2-3). The trimmed Lasso was used mainly as a reformulation tool (p. 3). The paper studies its structure, and its relation to other penalties, from the viewpoints of sparsity and robustness (pp. 3, 7).
key_idea: T_k is exact for large lambda (Theorem 2.3, p. 9). One uncertainty set (at most k perturbed columns, each with norm <= lambda) gives SLOPE under min-max (Proposition 1.2, p. 6) and the trimmed Lasso under min-min (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2, p. 15). The Lasso is the min-max case (Proposition 1.1, p. 5). The trimmed Lasso is the Lasso with k corruptions discarded (p. 17).
assumptions: Least-squares linear regression with a small eta*l1 term for well-posedness (p. 9, fn. 2). Bounded penalties mu*min{g(|beta|), 1} in Section 4, with unbounded ones treated as limits (pp. 17-18, 23-24). Test instance: n = 100, p = 20, k = 2, SNR = 10, Toeplitz covariance 0.8^|i-j|, ||beta_true||_0 = 10 (pp. 29, 43-44).
proof_devices: Binary representation of T_k (Lemma 2.1, p. 8), giving a big-M linear MIO whose LP relaxation is the ordinary Lasso for large M. Without a tuned M, SOS formulations prove optimality faster (pp. 28-29).
A Scholtes-type MPCC relaxation leads to the trimmed penalty (pp. 9-10).
Min-min versus min-max robust counterparts from one uncertainty set (Propositions 1.1-1.2, pp. 5-6; Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2, p. 15; p. 17).

Subsumption: clipped-Lasso optima are trimmed-Lasso optima (Theorem 4.1, p. 19). The converse holds iff a discrete convexity condition on optimal values holds (Theorem 4.2, p. 21). Strictness by a 2x2 example (Example 4.4, p. 23).

DC decomposition with alternating minimization: finite convergence to a local minimum at a linear rate, a result from [39] (Theorem 5.1, pp. 25-26). ADMM without a guarantee, with a closed-form sorting step (pp. 27-28; App. C.3, p. 43). Convex envelope (||beta||_1 - k)_+ (Lemma 5.3, p. 27).
experiments: A limited demonstration (p. 29): 100 seeds at p = 20. Relative optimality gaps of alternating minimization, ADMM and the convex envelope against MIO (Gurobi, no version given) along a lambda path. The heuristics do well for small lambda and fail as sparsity bites; ADMM is best and the envelope worst (pp. 29-31, 44). No runtime, recovery or out-of-sample study (p. 31). Code on GitHub (p. 7).
positioning: Extends the earlier trimmed-Lasso work [39, 43, 69, 72] from computation to structure (p. 3). Shows separable penalties subsumed rather than attacking them (p. 7). Sets robust statistics (Huber, LTS, total least squares) beside RO (pp. 3-5).
writing: Opens the robustness discussion with Huber's remark that 'robust' is a loaded word (p. 4). Three numbered contributions (p. 7). Computational claims are hedged (p. 29).
limits_future: No statistical properties, and no rigorous computational comparison (pp. 29, 31). Future directions: algorithms and statistical properties (p. 32).

method_links.note: Best subset is rewritten as an exact penalty with a binary representation and a certifying MIO. The authors print their own big-M weakness: the LP relaxation collapses to the Lasso, and SOS is faster. This is Tension T4 stated by the authors. Also full-text evidence for Heuristic 1: the robust problems behind the Lasso and SLOPE are identified, and the trimmed Lasso is derived as their min-min analogue (pp. 5-6, 14-17).
Heuristic upper bounds plus an MIO that keeps a suboptimality gap and can stop with a certificate. The duel is on objective gap only, at p = 20, with no runtime or out-of-sample comparison.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: min-max/min-min pairing of penalties from one uncertainty set
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The same column-perturbation set yields SLOPE as the pessimistic (RO) estimator and the trimmed Lasso as the optimistic (robust-statistics) one. The Lasso and LTS give a second min-min reading.

transferable: To interpret a new penalty, find the uncertainty set whose min-max counterpart is a known convex penalty, then take the min-min counterpart of the same set (pp. 5-6, 14-15).

To show a penalty family is strictly richer: rewrite separable bounded penalties as a minimum over trimmed problems (eq. (29), p. 18); characterize the converse by a discrete convexity condition (Theorem 4.2, p. 21); close with a tiny counterexample (Example 4.4, p. 23).
Compute the convex envelope to show what the LP relaxation of a big-M formulation keeps (Lemma 5.3, p. 27; p. 29).
Report heuristic quality as geometric-mean relative gaps to MIO optima across 100 seeds and a lambda path, listing all seeds and parameters (pp. 29-31, 43-44).

quotes.text: This gives an interpretation of the SLOPE and trimmed Lasso as a complementary pair of penalties, one under a pessimistic (min-max) model and the other under an optimistic (min-min) model.
However, by design, the MIO approach maintains a suboptimality gap throughout computation and can therefore be terminated, before optimality is certified, with a certificate of suboptimality.

title: Binary decision rules for multistage adaptive mixed-integer optimization
contribution: Proposes linearly parameterized binary decision rules y = Y G(xi), with an exact MILP reformulation via lifting, an exact convex hull and LP duality. Proves the general problem NP-hard and identifies polynomial-size structures (box sets, axis-aligned breakpoints). Extends to random recourse and multistage problems. Shows large scalability gains, at some loss of quality against the authors' earlier flexible rule.
problem_entry: RO+IO (AP testbeds). Multistage adaptive mixed-integer problems are #P-hard or intractable, so decision rules are used (p. 2). Real-valued rules abound and scale (Table 1, p. 3). Binary rules are near-optimal but unscalable (1.2), randomized, or K-adaptable for two stages only (p. 3). Goal: scalable binary rules usable alongside real-valued ones (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: y(xi) = Y G(xi), with G a vector of hyperplane indicators and Y integer (p. 6). Lift xi to (xi, G(xi)) so the constraints are linear in the lifted vector (pp. 8-10). Build the exact convex hull of the lifted support from one-sided limit points (Proposition 3, pp. 11-12). Dualize (Proposition 4, p. 13) to an MILP that gives the best rule for the chosen G (p. 13). The structure is fixed a priori; only the shape is optimized (p. 34).
assumptions: Expected-cost objective, with constraints for all xi in a polyhedral support with xi_1 = 1 (pp. 2, 5). The second-moment matrix is analytic or computed by offline Monte Carlo (p. 8). Fixed recourse; random recourse linear in xi (p. 20); multistage non-anticipativity (pp. 23-24). Tractable case: box sets with axis-aligned breakpoints (pp. 14-17); general polyhedra are handled conservatively (pp. 18-20). 30 random instances per setting (pp. 28, 32).
proof_devices: NP-hardness even with Y relaxed to reals, via an epsilon integer feasibility problem (Theorem 1, p. 10; Lemmas 1-3, pp. 34-38).
Lifting plus an exact convex hull of the nonconvex lifted support, built from one-sided limit points at the partition vertices (Propositions 1-3, pp. 9-12).
Robust counterpart by LP duality over the hull (Proposition 4, p. 13), giving MILP (2.20).
Separability for box sets: a product of marginal hulls with 2 + k(4r + 4) constraints (Proposition 5, p. 17). Y restricted to {-1, 0, 1} without loss, by induction (Proposition 6, pp. 17-18).
Random recourse lifted with G(xi)xi terms, at the same complexity (Proposition 7, pp. 22-23). In the multistage case the exponential growth in T is implicit (p. 26).
experiments: CPLEX 12.5, Core i5-3570, 8 GB (pp. 4, 27). Inventory: 15-20% better than static binary decisions at global, 1% and 5% gaps; global optimality is impractical for T > 20 and r > 9 (pp. 28-29). Against the flexible rule (1.2): 19-60% worse at r = 0 and 1-30% worse at r = 9, but seconds against up to 16,613 s (Table 3, p. 29). Gains saturate for r > 3; times reach 19,298 s at N = 4, r = 5, T = 50 (Table 5, p. 31). Knapsack: 26-36% gains; partial information reaches T = 25 with 1,300 binary rules, at up to 11,349 s (Table 6, p. 33).
positioning: A complement to real-valued rules, and the scalable alternative to the group's own rule (1.2) of Bertsimas-Georghiou. Builds on Bertsimas-Caramanis and on the lifting of Georghiou et al. (pp. 3-4, 34).
writing: Calls Theorem 1 'a rather disappointing result' (p. 10). The loss against (1.2) is stated in a table caption (p. 29).
limits_future: NP-hard in general, with exponential exact size (p. 13). Conservative for general polyhedra (pp. 19-20). Weaker than (1.2) (p. 29). Enrichment needs expensive solves (p. 30). The conclusion's 'horizons <= 50, ~5 min' (p. 34) holds for r <= 3 (357 s at N = 4, r = 3, T = 50) but not for r = 5 (19,298 s, Table 5, p. 31): Tension T6. Heuristic 4 evidence: the loss and the impracticality thresholds are printed (p. 29). No future-work list.

method_links.note: A class-keeping device (lifting, exact convex hull, LP duality) keeps discontinuous binary decision rules in the MILP class. The boundary is printed: NP-hard in general, exponential exact size, polynomial for boxes, conservative for general polyhedra.

Optimality is traded for scalability via knobs (breakpoints r, information restriction, termination gap). Tables show gain against time, saturation (r > 3) and the bad case against (1.2). The priced property is tractability, not a property the decision-maker wants.
Results at 1% and 5% gaps are shown next to global optima. The duel is against the group's own earlier rule, which wins on quality and loses on time. No out-of-sample test.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Gains over static decisions, and losses against the flexible rule, are tabulated against solution time across r, the information structure and the termination gap, with saturation for r > 3. S200 makes the same move.

transferable: Lift and hull: to keep indicator-based decision rules linear, lift xi to (xi, G(xi)), take the convex hull of the lifted support from one-sided limits at the partition vertices, then dualize (pp. 8-13).

With box sets and axis-aligned breakpoints, use separability (a product of marginal hulls) and restrict the integer coefficients to {-1, 0, 1}. In the tests this gives the same optima much faster (pp. 14-18, 29).
Solve the flexible but slow rule on a short horizon, read off its hyperplane directions, and use them to enrich the scalable rule's basis on longer horizons (pp. 29-30).
Restrict what a rule may observe to partial information (xi_s, xi_t). This cuts integer variables from s(r + 1) to 2(r + 1); tabulate the quality cost (p. 33).

quotes.text: Theorem 1 provides a rather disappointing result on the complexity of Problems (2.10) and (2.14).
The proposed decision rule problems have great scalability properties but do not perform as well compared to binary decision rules of type (1.2)

title: Optimization over continuous and multi-dimensional decisions with observational data
contribution: Prescribes continuous, multi-dimensional decisions from observational data by minimizing a weight-based ML prediction of cost plus penalties on its variance and bias. Gives finite-sample generalization and regret bounds, asymptotic optimality, and tractable formulations for trees and linear models. Shows gains on synthetic pricing and semi-synthetic Warfarin dosing.
problem_entry: DA+ML (AP: dosing, pricing). Optimize a known cost of an outcome that depends on the decision, from incomplete and confounded observational data (pp. 1-2). Earlier prescriptive methods assume decisions do not affect outcomes; kernel methods do not scale in the decision dimension; tree-ensemble MIO ignores uncertainty (p. 2); policy learning treats finite treatments (p. 3). Predict-then-optimize 'tries to learn too much' (p. 2).
key_idea: Choose z to minimize mu_hat(x, z) + lambda1*sqrt(V(x, z)) + lambda2*B(x, z): a weight-based cost prediction plus penalties on its conditional variance and on a Lipschitz bias bound (eq. (2), pp. 3-4). A lower-confidence-bound rule for offline exploitation, the reverse of UCB (p. 3).
assumptions: Ignorability (p. 2); honest weights (p. 3); bounded weights, Lipschitz within each of Gamma_n regions (p. 4); a bounded domain and a bounded, Lipschitz cost (p. 5). Homoscedasticity when variances are unknown (p. 4). Synthetic pricing with z in R^5 (p. 7). Semi-synthetic Warfarin data: 5,410 patients with known optimal doses, 99 covariates, and a simulated BMI-based physician policy (p. 8).
proof_devices: Uniform generalization bound: Bernstein's inequality conditional on the design (honesty), Jensen plus Lipschitz for the bias, then a nu-net in each of the Gamma_n regions and a union bound (Theorem 1, p. 5; pp. 11-12).
Regret bound that depends only on the variance and bias at the optimal action (Theorem 2, p. 5); asymptotic optimality (Corollary 1, p. 6).
Toy example in which the penalized regret is asymptotically strictly below that of predicted-cost minimization (Example 1, p. 6).
Tractability: per-leaf convex problems solved in parallel for trees; an SOCP for linear models, even with mixed-integer Z; coordinate descent for ensembles (pp. 6, 15).
experiments: Pricing: 100 training sets per n. At n = 2000, UP-RF gains $270 expected revenue over RF (Wilcoxon p = 4.4e-18); CART and Lasso fall below the plotted range (p. 7). Warfarin: fixed 4,000/1,410 split, 100 randomizations, dose MSE against the true optimal dose. Penalization improves CART/RF/Lasso by 2.2%/8.6%/0.5% (Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon). Comparators: a constant 35 mg/week dose, CRM with the true propensities ('always performed poorly'), and an unattainable lower bound (pp. 8-9). Lambda sensitivity checked (p. 16). No run times in the parts read.
positioning: Builds on Bertsimas-Kallus, Kao et al., Elmachtoub-Grigas and Misic (p. 2). Against continuous-treatment policy learning (Kallus-Zhou), prefers regression, which the authors believe scales better and needs no density estimation (p. 3).
writing: Theory motivates the penalties (pp. 4-5). The conclusion restates the contributions and names no limits or future work (p. 9).
limits_future: Homoscedasticity is assumed (p. 4). Lambda2 = 0 for regularized linear models 'for computational reasons' (p. 15). Ignorability and the simulated physician policy are assumed, not validated (pp. 2, 8). No future work stated (p. 9).

method_links.note: Learning and deciding happen in one model. Decisions are scored on decision metrics (revenue; dose error against the true optimal dose) against unpenalized predict-then-optimize, a constant-dose rule and an unattainable bound. The variance and bias penalties anticipate the Method 5 checkpoint (optimistic ML weights need a robust layer). Variant aspect: there is no owner's rule, and the historical policy is simulated.
The learner class is chosen so that the prescriptive problem stays tractable: per-leaf convex problems for trees, an SOCP for linear models.
Lineage only: the DA programme continues with a new student, after Bertsimas-Kallus and optimal prescriptive trees.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: pessimistic prescription (penalize variance and bias of a learned cost)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A lower-confidence-bound decision rule over a weight-based ML prediction, whose regret depends only on the uncertainty at the optimal action. An early instance of the robust layer later added to ML-weighted prescriptions.

transferable: Write the learner's prediction as sum_i w_i(x, z) c(z; Y_i) to get closed-form variance and bias proxies to penalize (pp. 3-4).
Pair a regret bound with a toy example in which the naive method's regret is asymptotically worse (Theorem 2 and Example 1, pp. 5-6).

Build a semi-synthetic observational benchmark from data with known optimal decisions: simulate a historical policy, fix the split in advance, and test over 100 randomizations with Bonferroni correction (pp. 8-9).
Tune the penalties without counterfactuals by imputing outcomes on a validation set with a random forest (pp. 4-5).

quotes.text: A key issue with the direct approach is that it tries to learn too much.
Because the predicted cost is penalized by V (x, z) and B(x, z), it does not matter how poor the prediction of cost is at suboptimal actions.

title: Robust transient analysis of multi-server queueing systems and feed-forward networks
contribution: Models interarrival and service times by CLT-shaped polyhedral uncertainty sets, giving closed-form worst-case transient system times for multi-server, tandem and feed-forward queues. Then averages the worst case over distributions on the conservatism parameters to approximate expected system times: within 10% of simulation for light tails, up to 30% for heavy-tailed 20-server queues. (Manuscript version read.)
problem_entry: SD+RO (AP: call centres, data centres, cloud). Heavy-tailed, long-transient systems never reach steady state (p. 2). Probabilistic transient analysis is by and large intractable (p. 2); there is no tractable transient G/G/m theory (p. 3); SDP bounds miss heavy tails and initial buffers (p. 3). The entry: extend the authors' robust steady-state framework (p. 4).
key_idea: Polyhedral sets on normalized partial sums, shaped by the generalized CLT, with conservatism parameters (gamma, Gamma) and tail index alpha (pp. 5-7). They give closed-form worst-case system times (Theorems 2-4, pp. 9-14). Then (gamma, Gamma) are treated as random (normal or stable), with Gamma = theta*gamma, and the worst case is averaged by a double integral (pp. 9-10, 15-18).
assumptions: FCFS, rho < 1, initial buffer n0 (p. 10). Assumption 1 sets, with multi-server service sets on blocks of m jobs (p. 7). Only an upper bound for Gamma_m < 0 (pp. 11-12). Gamma linear in gamma, because the exact distribution is hard (p. 17). Theta matched to Kingman for light tails, with an extended formula for heavy tails (pp. 17-18). GEV fit for tandems (p. 28). The heavy-tailed worst-case steady state is an artefact of the truncated tails (pp. 34-35). Simulation is the ground truth.
proof_devices: Lindley and Krivulin recursions; the worst case equals the queue without overtaking (Proposition 1, p. 11; App. A3, p. 47). Closed forms come from a one-dimensional optimization (p. 12).
Tandem worst cases by induction (Theorems 5-7, pp. 23-26; App. A1, p. 45).
Averaging: distributions on the conservatism parameters from limit laws, theta calibrated to Kingman's bound, and a double integral computed by discretization (pp. 15-18, 35).
Feed-forward networks as combinations of tandem paths, with a three-step algorithm (Propositions 2-3, pp. 36-40).
experiments: Average percent error against simulated expected system times: normal and Pareto primitives, rho 0.95-0.99, 1/10/20 servers, several n0 (Tables 1-2, pp. 18-20). Within 10% for light tails; up to 15% and 30% for heavy-tailed 10- and 20-server queues (p. 21). Tandems of J = 10, 25 and 50: mostly within 10%, with occasional outliers (pp. 30-32). Multi-server Pareto tandems omitted because simulation is costly (p. 32). Milliseconds per evaluation at a discretization of 1000 (p. 35).
positioning: Against transform and numerical traditions that give no general insight (pp. 2-3). Checked against Kingman (p. 9) and Morse (p. 34), and agrees with the probabilistic conclusions on heavy tails (p. 35). The reference list (pp. 41-44) has no Whitt-You or Goldberg-Li robust-queueing paper.
writing: 'Break new ground(s)' claims (pp. 1, 4, 6). A stated-joint rationale: RO as a natural framework for stochastic systems, tied to commercial solvers (p. 4). A practitioner-facing robust relaxation time (pp. 32-34).
limits_future: Heavy-tailed multi-server errors up to 30% (p. 21). Multi-server Pareto tandems omitted (p. 32). Theta for heavy tails set by an extended formula, not by matching (pp. 17-18). No future-work list (p. 40). Heuristic 4 evidence: the errors and the omission are printed. Context: critics later named choosing the sets, and tying them to the real queue, as open challenges [05 §4.5].

method_links.note: A problem owned by probabilistic queueing theory is rewritten as RO over polyhedral sets, giving closed forms rather than an LP/MIO. The boundary is partly printed: only an upper bound for Gamma_m < 0, and a heavy-tailed steady state that is an artefact. Tension T3 evidence: RO is claimed as the natural framework (p. 4), while the sets come from the generalized CLT (p. 6), the parameters get distributions (pp. 15-17), and the results are reconciled with probability (p. 35).
The one-knob conservatism Gamma is integrated out under a distribution from limit laws and calibrated to Kingman, not handed over as a price curve: the knob is set from theory.

A programme step with the same two co-authors, building on Bandi et al. (2012), and part of a broader RO investigation of stochastic systems. The manuscript is headed for Operations Research; the index lists Queueing Systems 2018.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: average the worst case over the conservatism knob
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Treat the uncertainty-set parameters as random variables with limit-law distributions and integrate the closed-form worst case to approximate expectations. This reduces transient analysis to a double integral.

transferable: CLT-shaped polyhedral sets: bound the normalized partial sums (sum_{i=k+1}^n T_i - (n-k)/lambda)/(n-k)^{1/alpha} >= -Gamma for all k, with alpha < 2 for heavy tails (pp. 6-7).
Calibrate the knob's distribution so that the averaged worst case matches a known asymptotic, here Kingman's heavy-traffic bound (p. 17).
Collapse a (J + 1)-dimensional integral to a double integral by fitting an extreme-value distribution to the sampled aggregate parameter (p. 28).
Report accuracy against simulation in grids over rho, the number of servers, n0 and the tail index, including where the method degrades (pp. 19-21, 30-32).

quotes.text: Robust Optimization (RO), arguably one of the fastest growing areas in optimization in the last decade, provides, in our opinion, a natural modeling framework for stochastic systems.
Errors for heavy-tailed multi-server queues seem to increase with the number of servers, with magnitudes within 15% for 10-server queues and 30% for 20-server queues.
